course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 3
unit.description: Follow the Seven Years' War, the road to independence, the Revolution, the Articles of Confederation and the Constitution, and the first political parties from 1754 to 1800.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes the British colonies in North America in 1754?
choices: Small, struggling settlements that depended on Britain for nearly all of their government and defense
A united federation of colonies with a common legislature that governed all colonial affairs from the city of Philadelphia
Growing, self-governing colonies that were expanding into the interior and meeting French and Native claims
Isolated coastal colonies with no contact with American Indian nations or with French settlements
questions.explanation: By 1754 the colonies were growing, they governed themselves through assemblies, and their expansion brought them into conflict with France and Native nations in the interior.
choiceExplanations: By 1754 the colonies had elected assemblies and a rapidly growing population.
The colonies had separate governments, and a plan of union proposed at Albany in 1754 was not approved.
By 1754 the colonies were growing, they governed themselves through assemblies, and their expansion brought them into conflict with France and Native nations in the interior.
Colonists were expanding into the interior and trading and competing with Native nations and the French.
questions.distinguisher: The dependence choice is close because Britain still ruled the colonies, but colonial assemblies already handled taxes and local government.
questions.subskillText: Identify and describe a historical context for a specific historical development or process.

questions.prompt: The competition among Britain, France, and American Indians for economic and political advantage in North America culminated in which of the following?
choices: The Seven Years' War, which Britain won and which removed France from eastern North America
King George's War, which ended with Britain returning the fortress of Louisbourg to France in 1748
King Philip's War, in which Native nations in New England attacked English towns in the 1670s
The American Revolution, in which French and British forces fought over the Ohio River Valley
questions.explanation: The rivalry over the interior led to the Seven Years' War, in which Britain defeated France and its Native allies.
choiceExplanations: The rivalry over the interior led to the Seven Years' War, in which Britain defeated France and its Native allies.
King George's War was an earlier conflict that ended without settling the contest for the interior.
King Philip's War took place in New England nearly a century earlier.
The Revolution was a war between Britain and its colonies, and it came after the Seven Years' War.
questions.distinguisher: King George's War is the near miss because it was also an imperial conflict, but the Seven Years' War is the one that decided the contest.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why British attempts to tighten control over the colonies after 1763 led to resistance?
choices: Colonial leaders had already decided in 1763 to seek independence and used new taxes as a pretext
British officials had banned all colonial trade with the Caribbean, which ended the colonial economy
The colonies wanted Parliament to take over their government because their assemblies had failed
Colonists who had long governed themselves through assemblies saw new taxes and controls as threats to their rights
questions.explanation: Colonists expected to govern themselves and tax themselves through their assemblies, so measures imposed from London collided with long-held expectations.
choiceExplanations: Most colonists first sought to protect their rights as British subjects, not independence.
Britain regulated trade, but it did not end the colonial economy.
Colonial assemblies had a long record of governing, and colonists wanted to keep them.
Colonists expected to govern themselves and tax themselves through their assemblies, so measures imposed from London collided with long-held expectations.
questions.distinguisher: The independence choice is close because the resistance ended in independence, but in 1763 colonists were still claiming the rights of British subjects.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a long-term consequence of Britain's victory in the Seven Years' War?
choices: France kept its claims east of the Mississippi River, so colonists stayed dependent on British protection
Britain gained a large empire and a large debt, which led it to seek revenue and tighter control over the colonies
Britain cut its military spending in North America, which left the colonies free of British regulation
American Indian nations gained a powerful European ally that helped them keep control of the interior
questions.explanation: Victory removed France but left Britain with new costs, so officials looked to the colonies for revenue and enforcement of imperial rules.
choiceExplanations: France gave up Canada and its claims east of the Mississippi in 1763.
Victory removed France but left Britain with new costs, so officials looked to the colonies for revenue and enforcement of imperial rules.
Britain kept troops in North America and tried to increase its regulation of the colonies.
Native nations lost the French as a counterweight to British expansion.
questions.distinguisher: The reduced-spending choice is close because Britain wanted to save money, but it responded by taxing the colonies rather than ending control.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: The writing of the Constitution in 1787 is best understood in the context of which of the following?
choices: A plan by Britain to reorganize the American state governments after the Treaty of Paris of 1783 ended the war
Demands from the western settlers that their territories be given power over the eastern states
Problems under the Articles of Confederation, such as war debt, trade disputes, and Shays' Rebellion
Public demand for a king to replace the elected legislatures that had governed the states
questions.explanation: Many leaders concluded that the Articles gave Congress too little power to handle the nation's debts, trade, and order, so they met in Philadelphia.
choiceExplanations: The Treaty of Paris recognized independence, and Americans designed their own government.
Western settlers wanted better access to markets and protection, not control over the East.
Many leaders concluded that the Articles gave Congress too little power to handle the nation's debts, trade, and order, so they met in Philadelphia.
Americans were committed to republican government and rejected monarchy.
questions.distinguisher: The Treaty of Paris choice is close because the treaty ended the war, but it did not shape the design of the new government.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a specific historical development or process is situated within a broader historical context.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a continuity from the colonial period into the early republic?
choices: Slavery remained legal and economically important in much of the South
Colonial governors appointed by the Crown continued to hold executive power in the new states
Parliament continued to regulate trade among the states under the Navigation Acts
The national government continued to collect taxes directly from the colonists as it had since 1764
questions.explanation: The Revolution ended Crown rule, but it left slavery in place, and slavery remained central to the economy of the South.
choiceExplanations: The Revolution ended Crown rule, but it left slavery in place, and slavery remained central to the economy of the South.
Most states limited their governors and removed the Crown's power to appoint them.
Parliament no longer governed the states after independence.
Parliament's taxes ended with independence, and the Articles gave Congress no power to tax citizens.
questions.distinguisher: The governor choice is close because states kept executives, but the Crown's appointment of governors ended.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following developments in the 1790s reflected disagreement over the power of the national government, economic policy, and foreign policy?
choices: The creation of the Articles of Confederation as the first government for the newly independent states
The formation of the first political parties, Federalists and Democratic-Republicans
The settlement of Jamestown as the first permanent English colony in North America
The passage of the Stamp Act as a tax on printed materials in the colonies
questions.explanation: Leaders disagreed about federal power, the economy, and relations with Britain and France, and the disagreements produced the first two parties.
choiceExplanations: The Articles were adopted in the 1770s and went into force in 1781.
Leaders disagreed about federal power, the economy, and relations with Britain and France, and the disagreements produced the first two parties.
Jamestown was founded in 1607, long before the 1790s.
The Stamp Act was passed in 1765, before independence.
questions.distinguisher: The Articles choice is close because it involved the power of the national government, but it belonged to the 1780s.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why the new United States had difficulty protecting its borders and trade in the 1780s and 1790s?
choices: France had taken over the Ohio country and refused to allow Americans to travel west of the Appalachians
American Indian nations had united into a single nation that controlled the Atlantic coast and the ports
The Constitution forbade the national government from making treaties or conducting foreign policy
British and Spanish power remained in North America, and Britain and France disrupted American shipping
questions.explanation: Britain kept forts in the Northwest, Spain controlled New Orleans and the lower Mississippi, and the wars of the French Revolution threatened neutral trade.
choiceExplanations: France had given up its claims east of the Mississippi in 1763.
Native nations resisted expansion in the interior but did not control the coast.
The Constitution gave the national government power over treaties and foreign affairs.
Britain kept forts in the Northwest, Spain controlled New Orleans and the lower Mississippi, and the wars of the French Revolution threatened neutral trade.
questions.distinguisher: The France choice is close because France was involved in the 1790s, but its involvement was at sea, not in the Ohio country.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.
